stories.title: Watch Your Car! Break-ins Hit Singapore Vehicles in Desaru
stories.headline_kid: Police in Johor caught a gang who broke into 17 cars, including four belonging to Singaporeans, at the popular Desaru resort area.
summary: Police in Johor, Malaysia, have arrested eight people accused of breaking into 17 cars across the state. Four of these cars belonged to Singaporeans and were parked at Desaru, a seaside resort area many Singapore families visit for holidays.

The suspects — four Malaysian men and four Indonesian nationals — are believed to have targeted vehicles left in quiet, open areas like carparks along empty roads, where fewer people were around to notice them.

This case is a reminder that even popular holiday spots can attract thieves, especially when cars are parked in isolated spots. Police have urged visitors to stay alert and avoid leaving valuables in view.
The Johor police worked quickly to catch the gang, showing how authorities in Malaysia and Singapore often share information to keep travellers safe across the Causeway.

lenses.me: If your family drives to Desaru or Johor for a holiday, remember not to leave things like bags or gadgets visible in the car.
lenses.family: Parents planning a road trip to Malaysia might want to park in busier, well-lit areas and double-check that the car is locked.
lenses.friends: Many classmates go to JB or Desaru during the school holidays — this is useful information to share with them.
lenses.nation: It shows how Singapore and Malaysia police can work together to protect Singaporeans travelling across the border.
lenses.world: It's a reminder that staying alert about safety matters no matter where in the world you are travelling.

stories.title: Indonesia's Forest Fires Are Now the Worst in the World
stories.headline_kid: Indonesia's forest fires are releasing more smoke and gas into the air than any other country right now — and that smoke could drift towards Singapore.
summary: Indonesia is battling one of its worst bouts of forest fires in years, with huge amounts of smoke and gas pouring into the sky from Borneo and Sumatra. Between Sep 1 and Sep 7, these fires released more carbon dioxide than fires anywhere else on Earth — over ten times the levels recorded in Russia, another country with major wildfires.

These fires happen when dry forests and peatlands (soggy, spongy land that stores lots of carbon) catch alight, often during the dry season. Once peatland catches fire, it can smoulder underground for weeks, making it very hard to put out completely.

The worst-hit areas are Kalimantan, part of Indonesia's side of Borneo, and eastern Sumatra. Smoke from these fires can drift across the sea and cause haze in neighbouring countries, including Singapore and Malaysia.
Environmental groups are watching closely, since strong haze can affect air quality, health and even flights in the region.

lenses.me: If the haze drifts to Singapore, you might need to wear a mask outdoors or stay indoors more, just like during past haze seasons.
lenses.family: Families may need to check the PSI (a number that tells us how clean or dirty the air is) before planning outdoor activities.
lenses.friends: Outdoor CCAs or school sports days might be affected if the haze becomes bad.
lenses.nation: Singapore keeps a close watch on Indonesia's fires since our air quality depends partly on wind direction.
lenses.world: It shows how actions in one country, like burning forests, can affect the health and daily lives of people in other countries.

stories.title: Singapore's Biggest Bank Faces a Billion-Dollar Lawsuit
stories.headline_kid: DBS, Singapore's biggest bank, is being sued for about a billion US dollars over its links to an old money scandal in Malaysia.
summary: DBS, Singapore's biggest bank, is being sued for about S$1.3 billion (roughly US$1 billion) over its links to the 1MDB scandal — one of the largest cases of missing government money in the world, involving Malaysia's state investment fund years ago.

The people suing DBS are called liquidators — people appointed to track down and recover money lost by companies. They believe money linked to the 1MDB scandal moved through DBS accounts, and that the bank should have noticed something was wrong.
DBS has firmly rejected the claim, saying it will fight the lawsuit 'vigorously' in court. The bank added that it has not set aside any money to pay for this case, showing it doesn't expect to lose.
This case will take time to go through the courts, but it shows how the effects of the 1MDB scandal, which happened over a decade ago, are still being felt today.

lenses.me: You might hear grown-ups talking about this in the news — it's about a bank you may recognise from ATMs around Singapore.
lenses.family: Parents who bank with DBS don't need to worry — this lawsuit is about old company matters, not about customers' everyday savings.
lenses.friends: It's a good topic to bring up if your class discusses money, banks or fairness in current affairs lessons.
lenses.nation: It matters for Singapore's reputation as a safe, trusted place to keep money and do banking business.
lenses.world: The case shows how banks worldwide are being held responsible for checking where big sums of money come from.

stories.title: Grandma's Tea Recipes That May Help With Haze Symptoms
stories.headline_kid: A TCM physician shares simple tea recipes that might soothe coughing, itchy eyes and runny noses caused by the haze.
summary: With haze affecting parts of the region, a Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) physician has shared some simple tea recipes that may help soothe common haze symptoms like coughing, itchy eyes and a runny nose.
Ingredients like snow pear, white radish, peppermint and snow fungus are known in TCM for their 'cooling' and soothing properties, which may help calm an irritated throat or nose caused by smoky air.

However, the physician warns that these cooling remedies aren't right for everyone. People with weak digestion or a 'cold' body constitution, as TCM describes it, should be more careful, since cooling drinks might upset their stomachs.

These teas are not medicine and won't cure illness, but they may offer some comfort while waiting for the haze to clear. It's always best to check with a parent or doctor before trying a new remedy, especially for young children.

lenses.me: If your throat feels scratchy on a hazy day, a warm cup of pear or snow fungus tea might feel soothing, but ask your parents first.
lenses.family: Parents might want to keep some of these simple ingredients at home during haze season, alongside masks and normal medicine.
lenses.friends: You could share this tip with friends who complain about itchy eyes or coughing when the haze rolls in.
lenses.nation: It shows how Singaporeans often combine traditional remedies with modern health advice during haze season.
lenses.world: It's an example of how different cultures have their own ways of coping with environmental problems like haze and pollution.

stories.title: Apple Unveils Its First-Ever Foldable iPhone!
stories.headline_kid: Apple has finally launched its first foldable phone, called the iPhone Duo, in its biggest iPhone change since 2017.
summary: Apple has just unveiled its very first foldable iPhone, called the iPhone Duo, at its big yearly launch event. This is being called the biggest change to iPhones since the iPhone X came out back in 2017.

A foldable phone is like a book — it can fold in half to become smaller and fit easily in a pocket, then unfold into a bigger screen for watching videos or playing games. Other phone makers, like Samsung, have made foldable phones before, so this is Apple finally joining that trend.

Apple also announced other new gadgets at the same event: the iPhone 18 Pro, an updated Apple Watch Series 12, and new AirPods 5 earphones. The event's theme was 'Surprise and shine,' and fans online had been guessing about the foldable iPhone for over a year.
These new gadgets will eventually be sold in Singapore too, most likely at a high price, since new Apple products are usually expensive when they first launch here.

lenses.me: You might see the iPhone Duo advertised at malls like Orchard Road once it's officially launched in Singapore.
lenses.family: Parents thinking of buying a new phone might wait to compare prices between the new foldable iPhone and existing models.
lenses.friends: This will likely be a hot topic among classmates who love talking about the newest gadgets.
lenses.nation: Singapore is often one of the first countries in Asia to get new Apple products, since Apple has stores here.
lenses.world: It shows how technology keeps changing fast, with companies racing to build the next exciting gadget.
